title: Cauchy sequences and complete metric spaces
section: Real Analysis ▷ The Completeness of the Real Numbers
terms: Cauchy sequence; complete space; metric completeness; closed subspace; total bounded- ness.

exposition.text:
A sequence is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there is N such that d(x , x ) < ε whenever m, n ≥ N.
m n
Every convergent sequence is Cauchy. A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence
n
converges to a point of that space; R and R with usual metrics are complete.
A subspace of a complete metric space is complete exactly when it is closed. The condition
d(x , x ) → 0 is much weaker than being Cauchy. Completeness depends on the metric, not
n+1 n
just the topology: distinct metrics producing the same open sets can have different Cauchy
sequences.
A metric space is totally bounded if for every ε > 0 finitely many balls of radius ε cover it. This
is stronger than boundedness. A metric space is compact exactly when it is both complete and
totally bounded: finite covers yield a Cauchy subsequence, and completeness supplies its limit.
A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit, by the triangle
inequality.

question.text:
On R, define d(x, y) = | arctan x − arctan y|. Which statement about x = n is correct?
n
(A) It is not Cauchy.
(B) It is Cauchy and converges to 0.
(C) It is Cauchy and has no limit in this metric space.
(D) It converges to every real number.
(E) The function d is not a metric.

solution.text:
The map arctan is injective, so d is a metric. Since arctan n → π/2, the sequence is Cauchy.
A limit x ∈ R would require arctan x = π/2, which is impossible.

question.text:
Which subset of R is complete with the usual metric?
(A) Q (B) (0, 1] (C) {1/n : n ≥ 1} (D) {0} ∪ {1/n : n ≥ 1} (E) R \ Z

solution.text:
The fourth set contains its only possible new accumulation point, 0, so is closed in com-
plete R and is complete. Each other set omits a finite limit of a Cauchy sequence of its own
points.

question.text:
In the usual metric on R, let x = log n. Which statement is correct?
n
(A) The sequence is Cauchy because |x − x | → 0.
n+1 n
(B) The sequence converges to one.
(C) The consecutive distances tend to zero, but the sequence is not Cauchy.
(D) The consecutive distances are bounded below by a positive constant.
(E) The sequence is bounded but divergent.

solution.text:
Consecutive differences are log(1 + 1/n) → 0. Nevertheless |x − x | = log 2 for every n, so
2n n
the Cauchy condition fails at any fixed ε < log 2. The condition must control every pair of
sufficiently late terms, not just consecutive pairs.

question.text:
Every Cauchy sequence in a metric space is
(A) Convergent
(B) Contained in a finite set
(C) Monotone
(D) Bounded
(E) Eventually constant

solution.text:
A tail lies in a ball of radius one about a fixed tail term. The finitely many earlier terms
can be enclosed by enlarging that ball, proving boundedness. Convergence additionally
requires completeness.

question.text:
A complete, totally bounded metric space is
(A) Necessarily a Euclidean interval
(B) Discrete
(C) Compact
(D) Necessarily finite
(E) Necessarily connected

solution.text:
Total boundedness lets one extract a Cauchy subsequence from every sequence by nested
finite covers. Completeness supplies its limit, giving sequential compactness and hence
compactness in a metric space.

question.text:
A Cauchy sequence (x ) in a metric space has a subsequence converging to x in that space.
n
What must follow?
(A) x → x, even if the ambient space is incomplete.
n
(B) The ambient space is complete.
(C) The sequence is eventually constant.
(D) Every point of the space is a subsequential limit.
(E) The whole sequence may diverge if the space is incomplete.

solution.text:
Given ε > 0, all sufficiently late terms are within ε/2 of each other. Choose a sufficiently
late subsequence term also within ε/2 of x. The triangle inequality puts every sufficiently
late term within ε of x. Completeness is not needed once one cluster limit is already
present.
